rad-lead: Several tabs do more than check that a radius of 6,371 km fits: they run the measurement backwards and let real data give the radius. Each line below is computed on the spot from its tab's data, with the reduction that tab defends.
rad-alt: Earth radius reconstructed by independent methods: for each, the median and the middle half of its values on a common kilometre scale, against the mean radius of 6,371 km
rad-seis: Earthquake surface waves: travel time over distance
rad-atmo-lamb: Pressure waves of Hunga Tonga, Krakatoa and the 1961 explosion, barometers
rad-surv: Reciprocal zenith angles between survey stations
rad-surv-tri: Angle sums of 1,600 survey triangles (USA, France, Cape, Britain, Russia)
rad-ct: Stars setting behind a mountain crest
rad-avia-eot: An aircraft's weight flying east and west (Eötvös)
rad-avia-fl: Airliner flight times and filed airspeeds
rad-dip: Al-Bīrūnī: a hill's height and the dip of the horizon, c. 1018 (quoted)
rad-note: Read the spread honestly. Each method has its own biases, explained in its tab: seismic waves run at different speeds under oceans and continents, the pressure wave's radius scales with a speed taken from the physics of the air, surveyors must correct for refraction, airliners fly detours that make the Earth look bigger, the Eötvös reconstruction undoes a published correction, the lunar laser and the Sun's Doppler shift read a local radius through an ephemeris, and the author's two measurements, one photograph and one filmed sunset, depend on the bending of light on the day and on a few pixels. Al-Bīrūnī's value is quoted from the literature, not recomputed. None of them was tuned to land near 6,371 km, and none of them gives the flat Earth a radius: on a plane the surveying, theodolite and dip methods return an infinite radius, and the others find no distances that fit at all.
rad-dip-own: The author's photograph of the sea from Caussols: the dip of the horizon, with that day's air
rad-obs-jan10: The author's sunset of 10 January 2026: the Sun touching a ridge
rad-cap: One line per measurement, on one kilometre scale, in two groups. Box: the middle half of its values; thick tick: the median; thin line: from the smallest to the largest value; black bar under the box: its total uncertainty. Dashed line: 6,371 km. In each group, the solid line and grey band are the weighted mean of that group's lines and its uncertainty. Grey lines are quoted from their author, not recomputed here, or shown without being counted. A plane has no radius: its answer lies off the scale, to the right.
rad-g-pure: Measurements: the radius never entered their data
rad-g-check: Checks: the radius entered their data at some point
rad-sum-pure: Measurements only ({n} of {k} kept): weighted by the inverse of their variances, R = {mean} ± {se} km, {z} standard errors from the mean radius of 6,371 km. χ² = {chi2} for {dof} degrees of freedom (Birge ratio {birge}). The most precise, {top}, carries {topw} % of the weight; one vote per measurement would give {plain} km. Set aside at more than {ks} standard deviations from the others: {excl}.
rad-sum-check: Checks, kept apart because the radius entered their data at some point, even when it was taken out again ({n} of {k} counted): R = {mean} ± {se} km, {z} standard errors from 6,371 km; χ² = {chi2} for {dof} degrees of freedom. Shown but not counted: {nc}. Set aside: {excl}. This second result is never mixed into the first.
rad-method: How each result is combined. Each line's uncertainty adds the statistical error of its median (from the scatter of its values and their number) to a systematic error measured in its own tab: the largest change produced by redoing it with the other reductions that tab presents. An alternative that itself used the radius, such as a wave speed measured with globe distances, is quoted in its tab but never used to size the uncertainty of a measurement. The lines of a group are weighted by the inverse of their variance; when they scatter more than their uncertainties say (Birge ratio above 1), the standard error is multiplied by that ratio, as the Particle Data Group does. A line is set aside when it lies more than three standard deviations from the weighted mean of the others, computed without it.
rad-moon-llr: Laser ranges to the Moon from Grasse (station's distance from the centre)
rad-orb-sun: Doppler shift of the Sun, HARPS-N (local radius at 28.75° N)
mo-lead: The same rule as for the radius: a measurement is pure when the quantity it gives, here the rotation rate Ω or the astronomical unit, never entered its data; the checks are kept apart.
mo-om-falls: Eastward deflection of falling balls (Guglielmini set aside)
mo-au-romer: Rømer reversed: 8,822 eclipses of Io, 1652–1983 (Lieske), six eras
mo-au-sun: Doppler shift of the Sun over three years, with the eccentricity from SDO
mo-au-star: Doppler shift of τ Ceti over sixteen years
mo-au-radar: Radar echoes from Venus, Millstone 1961, reduced with today's orbits
mo-au-psr: Twelve millisecond pulsars: timing (EPTA, NANOGrav) against interferometric latitudes (VLBA)
mo-au-transit1761: Transit of Venus, 1761: contact timings (Newcomb's collection)
mo-au-transit: Transit of Venus, 1769: 228 contact timings (Newcomb's collection)
mo-au-transit2012: Transit of Venus, 2012: contact III timed by amateurs (venus2012.de)
mo-sum: Measurements: Ω = {om} (the stars give 7.292 × 10⁻⁵); astronomical unit = {aup} from light alone. Checks: {auc} from Doppler shifts, the transits of Venus, radar echoes and pulsar timing. The accepted values are 7.292 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s and 149.6 million km.
rad-v-pure: Measurements alone: R = {mean} ± {se} km, from {n} independent methods, {z} standard errors from the mean radius of 6,371 km.
rad-v-check: Checks, kept apart: R = {mean} ± {se} km from {n} methods, {z} standard errors from 6,371 km.
rad-v-flat: A plane has no radius: the surveying, theodolite and dip methods return an infinite one, and the others find no distances that fit.
rad-f-nc-p: {nc}. The Eötvös line because its published data were corrected with the GRS80 radii (see the aviation tab). The lunar laser and the Sun's Doppler shift because each gives the distance of one station from the centre, which on a flattened Earth depends on latitude by up to 21 km, more than their few-km uncertainty.
mo-f-tycho-h: What the orbit measurements do not separate
mo-f-tycho-p: A yearly swing common to all stars, a yearly Doppler shift and a light time that changes with the season all show the observer moving relative to the stars and the Sun. An Earth at rest under a sky that swings in step every year reproduces the angles exactly (Tycho's arrangement); only the dynamics, why the whole sky would do that, chooses. The rotation measurements have no such twin: a ring laser or a falling ball feels the turning of the ground it stands on.
eyebrow: All the results · side by side
h1: One radius, one rotation, one orbit
lead: Every tab that runs its measurement backwards gives a number here: the radius of the Earth, the rotation rate, the size of the orbit. Each line is computed on the spot from its own tab's data. Measurements, where the quantity found never entered the data, and checks are never mixed.
rad-sat: Satellite Doppler: receivers' distance from the centre of the orbits
mo-alt: The rotation and the size of the orbit measured by each method: every value as a dot and the median as a tick, on axes starting at zero, where the flat models' predictions lie
mo-cap: Each method's values (dots) and median (tick), on axes that start at zero. Blue: measurements alone; violet: checks. Dashed: the accepted value, for comparison only. Orange: what the flat models predict, on the same axes: a plane at rest does not turn, and the flat model's Sun is a few thousand kilometres up. The ring lasers, the satellites and the sky agree to a few parts per thousand or better; the falling balls scatter, and the plot shows it.
mo-flat-au: flat Sun: a few thousand km
reel-alt: Animated showcase: a volcanic pressure wave crossing the globe, seismic waves stopped by the core, a ship sinking behind the horizon, the survey triangles appearing where they were measured, then a triangle on the globe whose angles add up to more than 180°, a Sydney–Santiago flight on a globe and on a flat map, satellites and their receivers, three eclipses of one saros landing further west each time, a Foucault pendulum
reel-cap: Eight of the site's methods in fifty seconds, drawn schematically: nothing here is measured, the numbers are in each method's tab. Click the animation to pause it.
reel-intro-a: The Earth is round, and it spins.
reel-intro-b: Not because we can see it: because it can be measured, in many independent ways.
reel-baro-a: A volcano explodes. Barometers around the world jump, one after another.
reel-baro-b: The wave closes up on the far side of the planet: its lap time gives the size of the Earth.
reel-seis-a: An earthquake sends its waves through the rock of the Earth.
reel-seis-b: Arrival times at every station fit a sphere, and the liquid core casts a shadow.
reel-avia-a: Sydney to Santiago: about 13 hours of flight.
reel-avia-b: On a flat map, at the same speed, the plane would be barely halfway.
reel-sat-a: Satellites fall around one single centre.
reel-sat-b: Their Doppler shift puts every receiver at the same distance from it.
reel-fou-a: A free pendulum keeps its swing: it is the floor that turns underneath.
reel-fou-b: At the pole, one turn a day; at the equator, none; in between, 15° an hour × sin(latitude).
reel-outro-b: One answer: a sphere of about 6,371 km, turning once a day.
reel-hh-a: A ship sails away. It shrinks, then sinks hull first behind the bulge of the sea.
reel-hh-b: On a flat sea it would only shrink: the hidden part grows like d²/2R.
reel-hh-exag: planet shrunk 100×, eye and ship enlarged 100×: same hidden part
reel-ecl-a: Every 18 years, 11 days and 7 h 43 min, Sun, Moon and node line up again: the same eclipse comes back.
reel-ecl-b: But in those extra 7 h 43 min the Earth turns about 116°: the shadow lands a third of the world further west.
reel-ecl-paths: saros 136 · the 2027 path of totality (NASA), carried to each member
reel-fou-t: seen from above the pole · {h} h
reel-tri-a: Surveyors measured the three angles of 1,600 triangles, from Maine to the Cape and the Baltic.
reel-tri-b: Their sum exceeds 180° by the area divided by R²: on a plane it never would.
reel-tri-big: drawn {x}× larger, where they were measured
